node.label: Adele Perry
node.date_label: ‘Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men’ 1995 · On the Edge of Empire 2001 · ‘Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History’ 2001 · ‘Women, Racialized People, and the Making of the Liberal Order’ 2009 · Colonial Relations 2015
node.description: A Canadian historian of gender, race and colonialism in British Columbia and the British Empire. In 1995 she argued that Canadian historians had explained the shortage of white women in the West with a 'scarcity model' and a 'volcano theory' of male sexuality that were 'based on essentialist understandings of both sexuality and race' and belonged to 'colonial discourse itself'. On the Edge of Empire (2001), which she said was 'initially inspired not by local experience but by a rich international literature on gender and colonialism', studied white miners' homosocial culture, mixed-race relationships and the schemes to bring white women to the colony, and found, in her words as reviewers quote them, 'a sharp disjuncture between colonial discourse and colonial practice on this edge of empire'. Reviewers placed it in whiteness studies and asked for more on Indigenous people: Sarah Carter (2002) wanted the 'social centrality and political agency' of Aboriginal peoples further developed, and Paul Orlowski (2002) found First Nations resistance 'lacking' and a 'binary racial divide' that set aside Chinese workers. In 2016 she described the 2001 book as arguing that British Columbia's history 'is best understood within a comparative framework of settler colonialism'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Adele Perry; “‘Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men’: Gender Imbalance, Race, Sexuality, and Sociability in Nineteenth-Century British Columbia” (BC Studies, 1995); “‘Fair Ones of a Purer Caste’: White Women and Colonialism in Nineteenth-Century British Columbia” (1997); “The Historian and the Theorist Revisited” (Histoire sociale/Social History, 2000); On the Edge of Empire: Gender, Race, and the Making of British Columbia, 1849–1871 (2001); “Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History” (BC Studies, 2001/02); “The Autocracy of Love and the Legitimacy of Empire: Intimacy, Power and Scandal in Nineteenth-Century Metlakahtlah” (2004); “Women, Racialized People, and the Making of the Liberal Order in Northern North America” (in Liberalism and Hegemony, 2009); Colonial Relations: The Douglas-Connolly Family and the Nineteenth-Century Imperial World (2015). Readings: Carter (2002); Orlowski (2002); Rutherdale (2002); the BC Studies forum on Colonial Relations (Clayton, Dussart, Devine, Ballantyne, 2016).
node.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14 in open copies. Her own words, read: '“Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men”' (BC Studies 105/106, 1995, pp. 27–44; pp. 27–33 and 42–43 read closely, the middle skimmed); 'Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History' (BC Studies 132, 2001/02, pp. 57–64, read in full); her reply in the BC Studies forum on Colonial Relations (190, 2016, pp. 106–114, read at pp. 106–108 and 112–113; a later reading). Reviews of On the Edge of Empire read in full: Sarah Carter (BC Studies 136, 2002/03, pp. 117–119); Paul Orlowski (Left History 8:1, 2002, pp. 119–122, in an Internet Archive capture, since the York journal site serves a browser check); Myra Rutherdale (Labour/Le Travail 50, 2002, pp. 324–326). Later reading: Tony Ballantyne in the 2016 forum (pp. 104–105). Unread: On the Edge of Empire itself (quoted only through its reviewers, with their page references), 'Fair Ones of a Purer Caste' (1997), 'The Historian and the Theorist Revisited' (Histoire sociale 2000; York site behind a browser check), the 2009 liberal-order chapter (title level), Colonial Relations (2015) and the other 2016 forum reviews except as noted. A search engine's summary first attributed the Left History review to Greg Dening; the PDF shows it is Paul Orlowski's (Dening reviewed the preceding book). Contested in period by Carter (2002) and Orlowski (2002) on Indigenous agency, by Orlowski on class and the omission of Chinese workers, and by Rutherdale (2002) on the metropolitan side; in 1995 she said her own analysis 'minimizes the subjectivity of First Nations people'. Post-2000 works are dated in labels and text.

proposed_edges.relationship: Gender and race in the making of a would-be white settler colony: British Columbia, 1849–71, where colonization and immigration were meant to produce a white, respectable society among a majority of Aboriginal people and failed to do so (2001), which she said was inspired by an international literature on gender and colonialism (no derivation from Wolfe's settler-colonial theory is established by the texts checked); later described by her as a comparative settler-colonial argument (2016)
proposed_edges.map_label: Gender, race and a settler colony, 1995–2001
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. 'Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History', BC Studies 132 (2001/02), pp. 57–64, read in full: On the Edge of Empire 'was initially inspired not by local experience but by a rich international literature on gender and colonialism. That through reading about imperialism elsewhere I came to see imperialism where I was is a suggestive comment on the convenient erasure of dispossession' (p. 58; the sentence ends 'settler consciousness' without a connecting word); 'The most remarkable pattern of silence probably concerns Aboriginal peoples' (p. 61). The 1995 essay (pp. 42–43, read) calls British Columbia 'a racially divided one controlled by a minority white population constantly engaged in a process of colonization' (p. 42). The book is unread; reviewers quote it: 'In contemporary newspapers and conversations, White British Columbians often long for the days when our society was unquestionably British … When we do so we long for a fiction of our own invention' (p. 201, as quoted by Carter, p. 117). In-period reviews. Sarah Carter, BC Studies 136 (2002/03), pp. 117–119, read in full: 'British Columbia fits within a broader context of European colonialism in that it was a settler colony where dispossesion [sic] of the indigenous societies and resettlement by a newcomer population were intertwined. While this is imperial history, it is not an example of the triumph of imperialism as in this era Aboriginal peoples remained demographically dominant and socially central' (p. 117); but 'The theme of the "social centrality and political agency" of the Aboriginal peoples of British Columbia could have been further developed' (p. 119). Myra Rutherdale, Labour/Le Travail 50 (2002), pp. 324–326, read in full: Perry shows 'how colonization and immigration worked in tandem in an attempt to create a White colony, while at the same time deliberately marginalizing the majority of the population, the Aboriginal peoples' (p. 325). Paul Orlowski, Left History 8:1 (2002), pp. 119–122, read in full: 'I found Perry's rendering of First Nations resistance to be lacking throughout much of the work, their portrayal emphasizing passivity rather than agency' (p. 121). Her own caution (1995, p. 43): 'my analysis minimizes the subjectivity of First Nations people'. No derivation from Wolfe is established by the texts checked: the 2001 essay cites Said, McClintock, Burton and Chakrabarty, not Wolfe, and the book is unread; the settler_colonialism roster already says Perry wrote 'earlier or beside' the paradigm. Later readings, labelled: in the BC Studies 190 forum (2016) she says the 2001 book 'makes the argument that British Columbia's history is best understood within a comparative framework of settler colonialism, echoing an assumption that undergirds Cole Harris's 1997 and 2002 books' (p. 112); Tony Ballantyne (2016, pp. 104–105) reads Colonial Relations (2015) as 'a salutary reminder of the limitations of work that follows Patrick Wolfe and Lorenzo Veracini in understanding "settler colonialism" as a fundamentally eliminationist project'.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The strand ('Gender, race, marriage and child removal in colonial British Columbia …') already lists her and On the Edge of Empire.

proposed_edges.relationship: Race in the history of white women and gender in the Canadian West: the 'scarcity model' and 'volcano theory' of gender imbalance traced to colonial promoters (1995), and white masculinity, mixed-race relationships and assisted female migration in colonial British Columbia read as the making of whiteness (2001)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. '“Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men”', BC Studies 105/106 (1995), pp. 27–44, read at pp. 27–33 and 42–43: Canadian historians used 'the "scarcity model" (the notion that women's experience improves commensurately with their scarcity) and the "volcano theory" of male sexuality (the assumption of a fixed quantity of male sexual energy)' (p. 27); 'a quarter-century of inquiry into women's history has produced little on the effect of a skewed demography on women's experience' (p. 28); its 'most clear example' is Jan Noel's 'New France: Les femmes favorisées' (p. 29 n. 4); both models 'are based on essentialist understandings of both sexuality and race. Practitioners of the "scarcity model" never compute aboriginal women (or, for that matter, men) into their arithmetical evaluation' (p. 30); they are 'integral not only to twentieth century scholarship, but also to colonial discourse itself' (p. 31), descending from Wakefield and the colonial promoters (p. 32); white women's experience 'was never determined by gender alone. British Columbia was a class society' (p. 42); 'While gender imbalance increased white women's opportunities for heterosexual contact, it restricted those economic and social possibilities not contained within the heterosexual nexus' (p. 43). On the Edge of Empire (2001) is unread; Orlowski (p. 119) quotes its aim, 'the importance of race to the social experience of gender in nineteenth-century British Columbia' (p. 8), and 'a sharp disjuncture between colonial discourse and colonial practice on this edge of empire' (p. 167, quoted p. 120; Carter, p. 119, uses the same phrase). In-period reception, read in full: Carter (2002): 'This book also makes a valuable Canadian contribution to "Whiteness" studies' (p. 117); Rutherdale (2002): 'At the heart of this imagined community was Whiteness' (p. 325), and the reformers' hope that white women were the 'imperial panacea' (p. 4, as quoted p. 326). Critics: Orlowski (2002) holds that she 'fails to invoke what Roediger calls the "wages of whiteness"', leaving 'a binary racial divide that runs through the entire book but did not run through colonial British Columbia', with Chinese labourers set aside (p. 121), and that her claim that 'class relations are central to social relations' receives little attention (p. 121); Carter (p. 119) asks for the North American setting ('This edge of empire had much in common with California'); Rutherdale's 'small quibble' is that the 'Home' and 'Away' relationship 'could be further probed' (p. 326). Distinct from the Van Kirk packet's edges on fur-trade women: this edge is the post-fur-trade settler colony and the critique of the scarcity model.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The only strand that lists her ('Comparisons: fur-trade women and gender on the edge of empire'). bodies_sexuality_law (Dubinsky and others) is the nearest topical alternative for the 1995 essay.

proposed_edges.relationship: Mixed-race relationships not to be explained by white women's absence: Perry's 1995 criticism of fur-trade historians, Van Kirk's 'brilliant account' included, for treating intermarriage as the product of that absence, and her 2001 argument (as Carter reports it) that such relationships were 'not confined to the fur trade' and that 'happy stories' of fur-trade marriages can 'obscure both coercive details and the larger brutality of colonialism'
proposed_edges.map_label: Perry: mixed-race unions beyond white women's absence, 1995–2001
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. 1995 (BC Studies 105/106, read at p. 30): 'Historians of the fur trade, while concerned with establishing the salience of mixed-race relationships, nonetheless explain their frequency as the product of white women's absence'; n. 8: 'For a brilliant account which ultimately suggests that the existence of mixed-race relationships was the result of white women's absence from the fur trade, see Sylvia Van Kirk, "Many Tender Ties" … Also see Jennifer S. H. Brown, Strangers in Blood … and Robin Fisher, Contact and Conflict'; n. 11 quotes Van Kirk: 'Had it been possible for fur traders to bring their wives out at an earlier date, it is doubtful whether intermarriage with native women would have been so extensive' (Many Tender Ties, p. 173); the 'volcano theory' 'holds that mixed-race relationships are at worst unfathomable and at best the products of abnormal historical circumstances' (p. 30). Qualifications kept: the criticism is of one explanation, not of the field; she calls Van Kirk's account 'brilliant' (p. 30 n. 8) and 'pioneering' (p. 43), and relies on it for the displacement of Aboriginal women (p. 43). 2001: the book is unread; Carter (BC Studies 136, p. 118, read) reports that 'Perry does not write a history of these relationships, noting the difficulties with available sources, but she does argue that they were not confined to the fur trade and could be found in the city, in the country, and in mining towns', and that she 'stresses the need to look beyond the "happy stories," such as the long marriage of James Douglas and Amelia Connolly, that can "obscure both coercive details and the larger brutality of colonialism" (62)'. In-period counterpoint: Orlowski (2002, p. 121, read) faults the book because 'the mixed-race couples in colonial B.C. had much to do with building alliances, sometimes between Hudson's Bay Company officers and the daughters of Aboriginal chiefs, a strategy that is not considered at all in the book'. No reply by Van Kirk or Brown was checked. Later reading, labelled: in 2016 (p. 113) she proposes thinking 'seriously about fur-trade colonialism as a distinct and meaningful practice of empire' (Colonial Relations, on the Douglas–Connolly family, is unread). Target: Van Kirk's person entry, since the criticism is of her explanation of intermarriage; her entry cites Perry's 2008 essay on her work only as a later reading.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: Retargeted at release (1.140) from native_newcomer/fur_trade_families_metis to the sylvia_van_kirk person entry released in the same batch: the critique is of Van Kirk's explanation of intermarriage. Release decision recorded in release/fixes-1.140.md (finding 11).

proposed_edges.relationship: Feminist and postcolonial work on gender, race and colonial categories (Stoler and McClintock, as she and her reviewers name them, with Said and Burton) as the 'international literature on gender and colonialism' that she said inspired On the Edge of Empire (2001), used with a caution about analysing 'white discourse and white discourse alone' (1995)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own words. 2001 (BC Studies 132, p. 58, read): the book 'was initially inspired not by local experience but by a rich international literature on gender and colonialism'; 'Edward Said's Orientalism contains the germinal insight that such stock knowledge functioned to inform and serve the centre rather than to understand the various peripheries about which, putatively, it spoke' (pp. 58–59); Burton's argument, as Perry puts it, that knowledge of margins should 'unpack the intimate wedding of historical scholarship to the nation-state' (p. 59, citing Burton in Catherine Hall's Cultures of Empire reader); Anne McClintock's 'anachronistic space' (p. 61); Chakrabarty 'convincingly argues' that history cannot be disaggregated 'from the politics of Western supremacy that produced it' (pp. 63–64). 1995 (p. 43, read), on scholars of colonial discourse who 'analyse white discourse and white discourse alone': the position 'contains an important critique of the intellectual conceit' in historians' attempts to represent the colonized, but 'it can also function to legitimize the neglect of First Nations histories'. In-period reviewers, their characterisations: Rutherdale (Labour/Le Travail 50, 2002, p. 325, read): 'Influenced by the work of Anne Laura Stoler, Perry argues that because "white and Aboriginal people shared ties, homes, children, and labour," they "challenged colonialism's foundational fiction"' (p. 123 of the book), and the book is 'informed by an international post-colonial, feminist, gendered, and Marxist analysis'; Orlowski (Left History 8:1, 2002, pp. 119–120, read): she is 'positioned within feminist postcolonial scholars such as Ann Laura Stoler, Robert J. C. Young, and Anne McClintock, all of whom she refers to in the book', and she uses 'discourse' in 'the Foucauldian sense', though she 'never defines' it (p. 121). The book itself is unread, so the influence of Stoler rests on the reviewers' statements. Stoler, McClintock and Burton have no atlas entries; Stoler is on the post roster (colonial_intimacies) and the gender roster (colonial_categories), Said has a person entry.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: Person entries carry no strands. On the source side the nearest strands are post/colonial_intimacies (Stoler) and post/imperial_knowledge (Said). gender/colonial_categories (Stoler, Amadiume, Oyewumi) is an alternative source; post is chosen because both reviewers and Perry frame the literature as postcolonial.

row.context: Criticised fur-trade historians, Van Kirk's 'brilliant account' included, for explaining mixed-race relationships as the product of white women's absence (1995), and argued that such relationships in colonial British Columbia were not confined to the fur trade (2001); later wrote the Douglas–Connolly family history Colonial Relations (2015).
row.works: “‘Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men’” (1995); On the Edge of Empire (2001)
